output.title: Design dashboards around the decision, not the screen
output.body:
Dashboard neglect is usually not a software problem first. It is a control problem: there is a status view or approval screen that should guide a recurring decision, but nobody checks it often enough to keep the work moving.

For a small business, the useful question is not whether AI can read the dashboard. It is what should happen when the owner does not look at it for two days. That is where the workflow breaks.

A bounded way to design against neglect is to separate three responses. First, add a reminder if the owner simply forgets. Second, automate the data refresh so the dashboard stays current without manual copy-paste. Third, only then consider whether the workflow can surface a decision, while keeping human approval in place for money movement and other high-risk calls. Human approval stays the gate.

The practical next step is simple: pick one recurring dashboard you already rely on and write one plain-English rule for it. What input arrives? What status changes? What action follows? If the rule is fuzzy, stop at data collection. If it is clear, scope the smallest pilot around one input, one flag, and one output. Bareni’s policy is to hand finished work back into your own accounts and tools, with no-lock-in as positioning, not a promise of magic.
